title: SK Hynix Q3 profit beats expectations, vows $75 bln in shareholder returns
full_text:
Investing.com-- SK Hynix clocked a stronger-than-expected third-quarter operating profit on Wednesday, with the South Korean memory chip giant outlining plans to return a total 100 trillion won ($75.5 billion) to shareholders this year.
Shares of the company jumped nearly 8% to 1,446,000 won in Seoul trade.
SK Hynix’s operating profit for the three months to September 30 jumped 632% year-on-year to 83.33 trillion won, handily beating Bloomberg estimates of 77.5 trillion won.
Revenue jumped 328% to a record 104.615 trillion won, while net income jumped 216% to 39.78 trillion won, the chipmaker said in a statement.

The company, which is among the world’s largest memory chip makers and one of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence boom, said it will pursue shareholder returns of 100 trillion won for the year.
This will comprise cash dividends of 30 trillion won or more, plus share repurchases and cancellations of 60 trillion won or more, including the 40 trillion won buyback it had announced in August and completed last week.
SK Hynix said it plans to fulfil its commitment to return 50% or more of free cash flow to shareholders, and that it will share most of the gains made on its investment in Japanese memory chip maker Kioxia Holdings (TYO:285A) back to shareholders-- representing a 10,000 won special dividend for the third quarter.
It announced a third-quarter cash dividend of 14 trillion won, or 20,000 won a share-- including the Kioxia payout-- and a share repurchase of 20 trillion won.
The company said that it expects the memory supply shortage to persist through 2030, amid increasing, outsized demand from AI.
It plans to ramp up production capacity, of both conventional memory, for AI servers, as well as high-bandwidth memory for advanced processors.
SK Hynix said it had secured long-term agreements with 14 major customers that cover more than 50% of its total production capacity for 2027 and 2028.
SK Hynix, along with rivals Samsung Electronics and Micron, represented roughly 95% of global DRAM production as of mid-2026-- a position that earned them massive, AI-fueled windfalls over the past year.
The company is a major supplier to Nvidia, and controls between 50% and 58% of global HBM supplies, according to Counterpoint Research.
SK Hynix’s American Depository Receipts-- which it had listed in a bumper offering earlier this year-- rose 4% in aftermarket trade. Micron added 3%, while Samsung Electronics jumped 8%.

title: Oil rebounds as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia overshadow diplomatic efforts
full_text:

title: Australia Q3 inflation quickens, bolstering RBA rate hike case
full_text:
Investing.com-- Australian underlying inflation accelerated more than expected in the third quarter, strengthening the case for another interest rate increase by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) at its meeting next week.
The consumer price index rose 1.3% in the September quarter, matching forecasts but accelerating from 0.6% in the previous quarter, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Wednesday. Annual quarterly inflation was 3.9%, matching expectations.
Get real-time updates on key economic indicators with InvestingPro
The closely watched trimmed mean measure of core inflation increased 1.0% quarter-on-quarter, in line with forecasts but above the RBA’s implied forecast of 0.8%.
Annual trimmed mean inflation accelerated to 3.7%, exceeding expectations of 3.6% and the previous reading of 3.6%.
The figures add to pressure on the RBA, which raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60% in September amid persistent inflationary pressures and rising oil prices.
"With underlying price pressures gaining traction, it looks increasingly likely that the RBA will put its foot on the brakes sooner rather than later," Capital Economics analysts said in a note.
The Australian dollar’s AUD/USD pair rose 0.3% to $0.704 after the data.
The central bank will meet on November 2-3 to decide whether to tighten policy further. Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said last week that the inflation outlook had deteriorated materially, highlighting the challenge of containing prices without unduly weakening economic growth.
Headline annual inflation also climbed to 4.3% in September from 4.0% in August, driven partly by housing and transport costs, including higher fuel prices.
With underlying inflation remaining well above the RBA’s 2%-3% target, the data could reinforce expectations of another rate hike.
"We now think there is a compelling case for another 25bp hike at next week’s meeting, whereas we had previously expected the Bank to hold fire," Capital Economics analysts added.

title: RBNZ unexpectedly holds rates at 2.75% in split vote, signals further hikes likely
full_text:
Investing.com -- The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held its official cash rate at 2.75% on Wednesday, defying expectations for a 25-basis-point increase as policymakers weighed easing headline inflation against persistent underlying price pressures and an uneven economic recovery.
The Monetary Policy Committee voted 4-3 to keep the OCR unchanged, with three members favouring an increase to 3.00%. The decision followed two previous rate hikes as the central bank sought to contain inflation risks linked to higher global energy prices.
New Zealand’s benchmark NZX 50 index fell 0.5%, while the kiwi weakened sharply, with the NZD/USD pair dropping 1.4% after the RBNZ’s decision.

Annual consumer price inflation slowed to 3.7% in the September quarter from 4.1% in June, coming in below expectations for 3.8%. However, inflation remains above the RBNZ’s 1%-3% target band, while core inflation measures have climbed towards the upper end of that range and price increases have become more widespread.
The central bank expects annual inflation to rise to 4.4% in the December quarter, largely reflecting higher fuel prices amid disruptions to global energy supplies.
Further tightening remains on the table
Despite holding rates, the RBNZ indicated that further tightening is likely to be needed, although the timing will depend on how the economic outlook evolves. Policymakers remain focused on returning inflation sustainably to the 2% midpoint of the target band over the medium term.
The committee was divided over whether to raise rates immediately or wait for more evidence. Members favouring a hike argued that persistent core inflation and the risk of price pressures becoming embedded in wage- and price-setting behaviour warranted action.
Those favouring a hold said the previous two increases provided time to assess their effects, while subdued wage growth and stable medium-term inflation expectations supported a pause.
The central bank also warned that geopolitical tensions, elevated energy prices and potential global financial stress could undermine growth.
The RBNZ said a further increase could be warranted if domestic pricing pressures fail to ease or broaden beyond what higher costs would normally explain. Conversely, persistently weak demand or a sharp global downturn could alter the outlook and eventually require monetary easing.

title: RBA Governor Bullock warns that inflation remains high, to debate more rate hikes
full_text:
Investing.com-- Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Michele Bullock said on Wednesday that local inflation still remained high, and that the central bank will debate next week whether four interest rate hikes were sufficient in bringing down prices.
Speaking at a parliamentary hearing, Bullock said inflation was “likely to remain elevated for some time,” citing pressures from the Middle East conflict, which drove up energy prices, as well as increasing capacity constraints in the Australian economy.
She noted increasing price pressures from the artificial intelligence boom, which drove up electronics and technology-related prices.
Get more breaking news on the RBA and Australian inflation by subscribing to InvestingPro
Bullock also said that despite a recent uptick in unemployment, the labor market remained tight.
“Against this backdrop, and despite growth in domestic demand slowing, a further period of subdued growth of aggregate demand is needed to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation down sustainably,” Bullock said.
“A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time,” Bullock said, noting that while higher rates were likely to be difficult for households, quashing high inflation remained a priority.
Bullock’s comments came as government data showed consumer price index inflation grew 3.9% in the third quarter, as expected. But core inflation– as represented by trimmed mean CPI– grew 3.7%, just above expectations and well above the RBA’s 2% to 3% annual target.
Separate data for September showed CPI inflation grew more than expected at 4.3%, remaining close to an annual peak of 4.6% hit earlier this year.
The RBA will meet next week, with markets wary of another rate hike after a cumulative 1.0% of hikes this year. The central bank struck a largely hawkish stance in the face of increasingly sticky inflation, with officials calling for a moderation in domestic growth to bring down price pressures.

title: Grand jury declines to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, source says
full_text:
By Andrew Goudsward and Kanishka Singh
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A federal grand jury has declined to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson who had provided testimony to a congressional panel that probed the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by President Donald Trump’s supporters, a source familiar with the matter said on Tuesday.
The Justice Department of the Trump administration has been investigating Hutchinson over whether she gave false testimony to the congressional panel. Hutchinson has maintained that her testimony was truthful.
A second source said the grand jury weighing evidence in the case had been meeting Tuesday but did not know if the indictment had been rejected.
A federal prosecutor told US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui during a court hearing that a grand jury in Washington had rejected an indictment but the prosecutor did not reveal in court the proposed defendant or charges.
Political experts have raised concerns about efforts by the Trump administration to target his critics and political opponents.
After weeks of Trump’s false claims that he had won the 2020 elections, his supporters had stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, in an unsuccessful attempt to prevent the congressional certification of those elections.
Trump pardoned nearly everyone criminally charged with participating in the 2021 Capitol attack on his first day back in office for a second term in January 2025.
Former Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith and his team secured an indictment in 2023, accusing Trump of plotting to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.
Smith dropped that and another case after Trump won the 2024 election, citing a Justice Department policy against prosecuting a sitting president.

title: StanChart raises 2026 income outlook after Q3 profit beats forecasts
full_text:
Investing.com -- Standard Chartered PLC (LON:STAN) raised its full-year income growth forecast on Wednesday after third-quarter profit beat expectations, as record wealth management income and strong trading helped the Asia-focused lender.
Pretax profit rose 27% year on year to $2.25 billion, above the $2.09 billion average estimate compiled by Bloomberg. Operating income rose 14% in constant currency, excluding notable items.
The bank now expects 2026 income growth to exceed its previous 5%-7% range and targets a return on tangible equity of around 14%, up from a prior goal of above 12%.
It also lifted its net interest income guidance to growth of about 4%, from low single digits, and switched its cost target to a cost-to-income ratio of about 60%, from an absolute figure of about $13.3 billion.
Chief Executive Bill Winters said the breadth and consistency of the performance reflected the strength of the bank’s franchise and its disciplined execution, giving management greater confidence in the revised outlook.
Wealth Solutions income rose 26% to a third consecutive record, driven by investment products and bancassurance. Global Markets income rose 21%, while net interest income rose 9% to $3 billion. Profit for the period rose 36% to $1.76 billion.
Goldman Sachs analysts said the quarter was a "beat and raise," with non-interest income the standout. They pointed to $20 billion of net new money inflows, which they said "reinforces the structural narrative behind Wealth."
The bank’s loan-impairment charge was $90 million, well below analyst expectations, helped by releases in its corporate and investment bank, Goldman said. It expects "the usual seasonal moderation" in the fourth quarter, with softer non-interest income, higher costs and more normal credit charges.
Standard Chartered, which like rival HSBC has expanded in wealth management to tap Asia’s growing affluent population, reported a liquidity coverage ratio of 154%. Its common equity tier 1 ratio eased to 13.8% from 14.2% a year earlier.
Goldman said new guidance on a Basel 3.1 risk-weighted asset headwind is largely offset by a 30 basis-point cut in the bank’s Pillar 2A requirement.

title: Ambani’s Jio becomes India’s second-most valuable firm in $131.5 billion debut
full_text:
By Vibhuti Sharma and Aditya Kalra
MUMBAI, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Shares of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Jio Platforms soared 21% in their Mumbai debut on Wednesday, making it India’s second-largest company by market capitalisation, valued at about $131.5 billion.
The listing, the first for the Reliance conglomerate in two decades, furthers Ambani’s plan to turn Reliance from an oil-and-chemicals conglomerate into an "everything company" spanning consumer products and technology.
Jio, whose telecoms business serves more than 530 million customers, is backed by Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google. Its user numbers are second only to China Mobile on the basis of single-country subscribers.
The listing ceremony on Wednesday in Mumbai was attended by members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh’s eldest son, Akash, who is Jio’s managing director. Before walking to the stage to speak, he touched his parents’ feet, a traditional gesture of respect.
While all three children of the senior Ambani gave speeches, Mukesh sat in the audience, visibly emotional and in tears.
Mukesh Ambani, Asia’s richest person according to Forbes magazine, has spent years shaping a succession plan that was intended to avoid a repeat of the public feud with his younger brother, Anil, that followed their father Dhirubhai’s death in 2002 without a will.
To celebrate the listing, Reliance is hosting a celebration for employees at its large office near Mumbai, with jam sessions and other performances planned, an internal memo showed.
Jio’s stock opened at 1,358 rupees a share, compared with its 1,119-rupee offer price. Its market capitalisation overtook those of telecom firm Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank, making it the second-largest Indian firm by that metric.
"The IPO price offered a valuation entry point; the listing price reflects a much greater degree of optimism," said Aishvarya Dadheech, founder of Fident Asset Management.
’THANK YOU, INDIA’
Several brokerages see a potential upside for the Jio stock, but they flagged competition, heavy capital spending and changes in India’s telecom rules, including those related to spectrum, licensing and fees.
"Jio has had a strong debut even despite geopolitical issues and turbulent market conditions ... the revenues and earnings will lead the stock here onwards," said Kranthi Bathini, equity strategist at WealthMills Securities.
The Ambani family rang the IPO bell on stage at the National Stock Exchange in Mumbai. Mukesh Ambani watched as Anant traced Reliance’s and Jio’s legacies and journey in a speech at the ceremony.
Major Indian newspapers on Wednesday carried front-page ads from Reliance Jio, saying, "Thank you, India."
India has become the world’s busiest IPO market this year in terms of the number of deals, with 246 listings so far, though it ranked fourth by money raised at $13.5 billion, behind the US, mainland China and Hong Kong, LSEG data showed.
Including Jio Platforms’ record IPO would lift India above Hong Kong’s $15.4 billion, according to Reuters calculations.
Despite its size, Jio Platforms’ IPO was not a record payday for its bankers. Its 19 bankers will split about $20.7 million, or 0.65% of the offer, roughly half the 1.3% that sources said Hyundai Motor India paid to its bankers in 2024.
WEALTH GENERATOR
The Jio listing is the Ambanis’ latest turn at the stock market. Dhirubhai Ambani, Mukesh’s father and Reliance’s founder, took the company public in 1977 with an offering aimed at small retail investors, which was widely credited with helping build India’s equity culture.
Jio comes from a stable that Indian investors have long backed: parent Reliance Industries has returned about 900% since 2006, ahead of the Nifty’s 685%, LSEG data shows, and is often seen as a buy-and-hold staple in retail portfolios.
After the ceremony, people waved flags bearing the Jio logo next to the National Stock Exchange’s bull statue, where the Ambani family posed for pictures.

title: Rémy Cointreau sales beat estimates on cognac strength
full_text:
Investing.com - Remy Cointreau (EPA:RCOP) on Wednesday reported second-quarter sales that exceeded analyst expectations, driven by strong cognac performance in Asia-Pacific, though its liqueurs business continued to face headwinds from U.S. distribution changes.
The French spirits maker posted organic sales growth of 4.2% in the second quarter ended September, beating the analyst consensus of 3.6%. Total sales reached €287.7 million, compared to the consensus estimate of €280.8 million. For the first half, organic sales rose 2.9%, reaching €510.9 million, up from €489.6 million in the prior-year period, representing a 4.4% increase on a reported basis.
The cognac division delivered organic growth of 12.4% in the second quarter, surpassing the analyst estimate of 8.9%. Growth was driven primarily by accelerated shipments to China ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival and continued momentum across the rest of Asia. The liqueurs and spirits division declined 7.4% organically in the second quarter, missing the consensus estimate of a 4.7% decline, as sales were affected by destocking in the U.S. following distribution changes.
"The Group’s objective of achieving a slight organic improvement in Current Operating Margin is thus unchanged," the company stated, while noting that approximately €15 million in tariff savings would be fully reinvested to support growth.
Rémy Cointreau revised its tariff impact estimate to approximately €5 million on current operating profit, down from €20 million previously. The reduction reflects lower U.S. tariffs on European imports, which fell to 10% from 15%, and €6.4 million in tariff refunds relating to fiscal 2025-26 recognized in the first half.
The company also updated its currency impact forecast, now expecting a positive effect of around €15 million on sales and between €3 million and €5 million on current operating profit, compared to previous estimates of negative €15 million and negative €5 million to €8 million, respectively.
For the full fiscal year 2026-27, Rémy Cointreau (EURONEXT:RCO) confirmed its guidance for a return to sustainable organic sales growth, with momentum expected to strengthen progressively throughout the year. The company aims to maintain leverage below 3.5 times net debt to EBITDA at March 31, 2027.
On September 30, Rémy Cointreau completed its inaugural €250 million hybrid bond issue with a 6.75% fixed coupon, which will be recognized entirely as equity.

title: Alphabet, Microsoft to report; Fed decision ahead - what’s moving markets
full_text:
Investing.com - Futures linked to the main U.S. stock indices hover around both sides of the flatline, as investors prepare for a raft of key tech sector earnings and a key Federal Reserve interest rate decision. Alphabet and Microsoft are scheduled to kick off a parade of major tech-sector earnings after the closing bell, while South Korea’s SK Hynix reports a sharp jump in quarterly operating profit. Meanwhile, traders will be searching for clues into the Fed’s rate outlook following the central bank’s latest policy announcement.
1. Futures mixed
U.S. stock futures were mixed on Wednesday. By 04:02 ET (08:02 GMT), the S&P 500 futures contract had risen by 10 points, or 0.1%, Nasdaq 100 futures had climbed by 173 points, or 0.6%, and Dow futures had dipped by 117 points, or 0.2%.
The main averages on Wall Street all advanced in the prior session, with tech stocks in particular powering a 1.18% jump in the Nasdaq Composite. A slew of recent artificial intelligence funding deals, as well as Claude-maker Anthropic’s long-awaited IPO filing earlier this week, have helped to soothe jitters around massive debt-fueled spending on AI infrastructure.
"[I]nvestors continue to celebrate the AI funding announcements that hit the tape over the last 36 hours [...] as these demonstrate that plenty of money still exists to underwrite the data center bonanza," analysts at Vital Knowledge wrote in a note.
At the same time, the quarterly corporate earnings season is roughly a third over. Results have largely been "decent" thanks to resilient demand, cost controls, and price hikes, the Vital Knowledge analysts said.
2. Big-name tech earnings loom large
Although the AI anxieties of recent weeks were given a reprieve this week, a major test of the AI boom is due to come after the closing bell.
Google-owner Alphabet and software giant Microsoft are set to headline the slate of post-market earnings -- and potentially shed more light on the AI spending outlook among some of the world’s largest companies.
In particular, traders are hunting for any signs of possible returns from Big Tech’s planned expenditures -- in some cases ranging into the hundreds of billions of dollars -- on the data centers and chips underpinning AI systems.
Altogether, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon -- which reports after the bell on Thursday -- are aiming to shell out as much as $600 billion in capital expenditures this year alone.
Whether investors will welcome or balk at an increase to those spending forecasts may be a central question when the firms report this week. Earlier this month, an uptick in Facebook-owner Meta Platforms’ spending plans cast a pall over otherwise strong results, sending shares down a day later. Meta’s stock is now down by more than 4% so far this year.
"The more skeptical the market gets about AI returns, the harder it becomes to justify today’s pace of spending. Meta is a good example: the core business was shown to be strong, but with capex hitting nearly $34 billion in a single quarter, the market increasingly needs to see the ROI from that investment," said Jake Behan, Head of Capital Markets at Direxion.
3. SK Hynix operating profit surges
To that end, SK Hynix posted a stronger-than-expected third-quarter operating profit on Wednesday, with the South Korean memory chip giant outlining plans to return a total of 100 trillion won ($75.5 billion) to shareholders this year.
Shares of the company jumped over 10% in Seoul trade.
SK Hynix’s operating profit for the three months to September 30 surged 632% versus a year ago to 83.33 trillion won, handily beating Bloomberg estimates of 77.5 trillion won.
Revenue spiked 328% to a record 104.615 trillion won, while net income jumped 216% to 39.78 trillion won, SK Hynix said in a statement.
The company, which is among the world’s largest memory chipmakers and has been a major beneficiary of the AI era, said it will pursue shareholder returns of 100 trillion won for the year.
4. Fed decision ahead
How investors feel about AI debt deals and spending binges could also be swayed by Wednesday’s all-important Fed interest rate decision.
The central bank is tipped to leave rates unchanged after policymakers lifted borrowing costs for the first time since 2023 in September. However, there is currently a three-in-four chance that the Fed opts to raise rates again at its final meeting of the year in December.
For that reason, analysts have suggested that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s post-decision press conference will receive especially close scrutiny. Yet don’t hold your breath for clear-cut guidance: Warsh has long resisted laying out forward guidance.
Still, some of Warsh’s colleagues at the Fed have indicated that more hikes may be necessary to quell elevated inflationary pressures.
For tech, more policy tightening could "raise the cost of funding the AI buildout while simultaneously raising the hurdle for the returns needed to justify it," Direxion’s Behan flagged.
5. U.S. warns Gulf countries of Iran war renewal after midterms - WSJ
A key driver of rate expectations in recent months have been oil prices, which have soared largely because of disruptions to Middle East supplies following the outbreak of the Iran war in late February.
The increase in crude has pushed up the costs of items like diesel and gasoline. Economists are now on the lookout for any indication that these price jumps, which can impact everything from transportation expenses to consumer gas prices, are feeding into other goods and services.
Although markets have cheered a fresh diplomatic effort to avoid fresh fighting in Iran, the conflict has spread across the Middle East and has shown little sign of de-escalating. Indeed, the U.S. has told Gulf Arab countries to be ready for a short, intense military campaign following the American midterm elections in November, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Benchmark Brent crude futures were last higher by 1.2% at $115.29 a barrel.

title: Europe gas climbs to fresh 2022 peaks as Houthi strikes on Saudi energy hubs
full_text:
Investing.com - European wholesale natural gas prices climbed to fresh 2022 highs on Wednesday, as renewed ballistic missile and drone strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement against critical Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure threatened to derail diplomatic de-escalation efforts, compounding fears over global fuel security ahead of peak winter heating demand.
The front-month Dutch TTF contract, the benchmark for continental Europe, advanced 1.2% to 97.35 euros per megawatt-hour (MWh), trading at its highest level in roughly four years.
Across the Channel, the British equivalent NBP futures contract gained 1.5% to 241.00 pence per therm, also touching a new 2022 high-water mark and extending its winning streak to a sixth consecutive session.
The renewed rally across European natural gas curves followed a sharp escalation in regional hostilities that overshadowed nascent diplomatic engagement in Tehran.
Delegations from Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan had gathered with senior Iranian officials in the Iranian capital on Monday, issuing joint statements confirming an agreement to pursue sustained dialogue aimed at restoring regional peace and security.
However, any optimism generated across global trading desks quickly evaporated after the Houthi movement announced on Tuesday that it had targeted Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura oil refinery - the kingdom’s largest refining complex and crude export terminal - with a ballistic missile.
The strike followed earlier coordinated attacks this week on pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s vital East-West Crude Oil Pipeline, as well as Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
Because the 1,200-kilometer East-West pipeline represents the primary conduit allowing energy supplies to bypass the heavily contested Strait of Hormuz by transporting volumes to Red Sea ports, the attacks highlighted the extreme vulnerability of alternative supply corridors.
With commercial navigation through the Strait of Hormuz already severely disrupted by the wider conflict involving Iran, energy traders moved swiftly to price out prospective de-escalation discounts.
Persian Gulf bottlenecks amplify pre-winter LNG Deficits
The persistent threat to Middle Eastern energy infrastructure has effectively shut down normal seaborne Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) trade routes, leaving European utilities structurally short of replacement volumes.
With LNG carriers forced to circumnavigate Africa via the Cape of Good Hope, transit times have extended by roughly 10 to 14 days, raising shipping freight costs and keeping spot deliveries to European regasification terminals down by nearly 80% compared with year-ago levels.
The upward price pressure is reinforced by exceptionally fragile domestic inventory cushions across the European Union.
Data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) indicates that EU underground storage caverns sit at approximately 74.6% of nominal capacity. This marks the lowest regional storage trajectory for late October in records dating back to 2009, lagging significantly behind the 86% historical five-year seasonal average and the 95%+ fill levels logged during the comparable period last year.
With meteorological services signaling an early arrival of sub-seasonal temperatures across Northern and Central Europe in early November, utilities face premature withdrawals from already depleted salt caverns.

title: UBS’s new Brent price forecasts as Middle East supply risk supports oil prices
full_text:
Investing.com -- UBS raised its Brent crude forecasts and now expects prices to stay near $110 a barrel at year-end, citing volatile Middle East supply, falling inventories and record freight rates.
In a new note, strategist Giovanni Staunovo lifted the year-end Brent target to $110 from $100. The bank also raised its March 2027 forecast to $95 from $90, its June 2027 forecast to $90 from $85, and its September 2027 forecast to $85 from $80. UBS widened the WTI discount to Brent to $10 for December, while keeping a $4 discount for 2027.
“Hence, we retain a moderately constructive near-term outlook for crude oil,” Staunovo wrote.
Middle Eastern crude flows have recovered to close to 18.8 million barrels per day in early October, compared with 19.9 million before the conflict.
However, at least 30 attacks on ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz were reported in October, the highest monthly number on record.
“Higher oil flows have not translated into a normalization of the market: Vessels remain exposed to attacks, insurance and freight costs have risen sharply, and increased ship-to-ship transfers required to cross the Strait of Hormuz are absorbing tanker capacity,” the strategist said.
He added that global visible oil inventories have fallen by slightly more than 500 million barrels since February, mostly from strategic reserve releases. With those releases now largely complete, UBS expects commercial stocks to decline more sharply.
Tanker freight rates from the Middle East to China have reached $30 to $40 a barrel, compared with $1 to $3 over the previous decade. Chinese crude imports are also recovering, potentially reaching 10 million barrels per day in October.
UBS concluded: “Uncertainty around our forecasts remains elevated, reflecting both the unpredictable nature of the Middle East conflict, and the pace of recovery in Gulf production and global oil demand.”

title: European banks beat profit forecasts, Brazil overshadows Santander
full_text:
By Ariane Luthi, Tom Sims, Mateusz Rabiega and Jesús Aguado
ZURICH/FRANKFURT/PARIS/MADRID, Oct 28 (Reuters) - European banks went some way to easing investor concerns about slowing earnings momentum on Wednesday as a string of lenders reported stronger-than-expected quarterly results, pushing back against fears that a years-long profit boom is losing steam.
Deutsche Bank, BNP Paribas, Standard Chartered and Santander all beat third-quarter profit forecasts, while UBS accelerated a share buyback after reporting earnings broadly in line with expectations.
Santander’s results were clouded by weaker earnings and higher provisions in Brazil, a key market where the surprise re-election of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has rattled financial markets.
European banks have enjoyed record profits since 2024, fuelled by higher interest rates, sending their shares soaring. But banking stocks have fallen about 10% over the past month amid concerns over lenders’ exposure to euro zone government debt and a weakening economic outlook.
HSBC also unsettled investors on Tuesday after reporting weaker-than-expected revenue growth, with some analysts pointing to rising competition for deposits and slowing interest income as signs the earnings boost from higher rates may be fading.
Shares were mixed on Wednesday. Deutsche Bank was up 3.4% and Standard Chartered up 3.7%, while UBS fell 1.1% and Santander dropped 4.2%. The European banking index was flat, in line with the broader market.
The reaction to HSBC’s results, which sent its shares down more than 5% on Tuesday, highlighted how recent strong performance has raised the bar for European lenders, even as the Iran war has complicated the outlook for inflation and interest rates.
BNP BOOSTED BY EQUITY TRADERS
Investment banking divisions at European lenders generally held up well during the quarter, in some cases outperforming Wall Street rivals despite a softer environment for fixed-income, currency and commodities trading.
BNP Paribas said a surge in equities trading, fuelled by volatile markets, helped lift third-quarter profit 14% to €3.46 billion ($3.85 billion). The French bank also announced a €1.3 billion share buyback and played down the impact of rising French government bond yields on its business.
Citi analysts described the figures as a "solid set of results", helped in part by the investment bank.
At Deutsche Bank, revenue from fixed-income and currency trading fell 3%, in line with expectations and less severe than the 5% decline reported by US peers.
Overall, Germany’s largest lender posted a 2% rise in profit, beating forecasts, helped by strength in its retail and corporate banking businesses.
"We are delivering on our commitments and are firmly on track to meet our 2026 objectives," CEO Christian Sewing said.
Standard Chartered also struck an upbeat tone, raising its income and profitability targets after third-quarter profit comfortably beat estimates, supported by its wealth and global markets businesses.
UBS RESULTS SEEN AS MIXED
UBS, Switzerland’s largest bank, reported net profit of $2.69 billion for the three months, up 8% from a year earlier and broadly in line with the $2.71 billion expected in a company-compiled consensus forecast.
UBS repurchased $1.8 billion of shares during the quarter and plans to complete its $3 billion buyback programme by February, ahead of its previous target of mid-2027.
RBC analysts described the UBS results as "mixed with underlying revenues broadly in line with estimates but GWM (Global Wealth Management) revenues below expectations".
Despite weakness in Brazil, Santander reported a 19% rise in underlying third-quarter net profit, helped by contributions from recently acquired lenders in Britain and the US.
"At a time of heightened volatility, our combination of at-scale global businesses and diversification across Europe and the Americas is a distinctive source of strength," Executive Chair Ana Botin said.

title: US bans imports from BGI Genomics, MGI Tech, citing ties to forced labor in Xinjiang

By Karen Freifeld
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The United States on Wednesday banned imports from three Chinese genomics companies over their alleged roles in enabling the forced labor of Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities in China’s Xinjiang region.
BGI Genomics Co. Ltd, MGI Tech Co Ltd and Shenzhen BGI Technology Co Ltd, which the US says is also known as the BGI Group, were added to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List, according to the Department of Homeland Security.
The list identifies entities that use or facilitate the use of forced labor of Uyghurs and other minorities, or source material from the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
US Customs and Border Protection is instructed to stop goods from companies on the list from entering the US unless exporters can rebut the presumption they were made with forced labor.
The US and human rights groups have accused Chinese authorities of establishing internment camps in Xinjiang, where Uyghurs and other religious and ethnic minority groups are subject to forced labor and other abuses. Beijing has denied the allegations.
BGI Group and BGI Genomics conduct genetic testing in the region, working with the government to facilitate the recruitment, transport, transfer or receiving of forced labor, the Homeland Security Department said. MGI Tech provides equipment and related support to the government to conduct the testing, the department said.
The US government believes BGI Group tests genetic material of people from the region as well as that of plants and animals.
Shenzhen-based MGI Tech rejected the allegations, saying they are inconsistent with the facts. It added that business activities in the US represent a limited part of its overall business.
"We have zero tolerance for forced labor in any form," the company said in a statement.
Neither BGI Genomics nor BGI Group immediately responded to requests for comment. In the past, BGI Group has denied assertions that it participated in the collection, storage or analysis of personal genetic information to infringe on human rights. It also has denied supporting the surveillance of minorities.
The Chinese embassy in Washington also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
BAN COMES DURING US-CHINA TRADE TRUCE
The US imposed the ban during a fragile trade truce between China and the United States.
China banned imports of sequencing equipment from San Diego-based Illumina in March 2025, minutes after an additional 10% US tariff on Chinese goods took effect. Illumina said in November 2025 that China’s Ministry of Commerce said it would lift the ban, but that the company would remain on China’s Unreliable Entities List, meaning purchases of its instruments would still require government approval.
Homeland Security, which oversees the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List, on Wednesday posted the additions on the Federal Register, the US government’s official daily journal. With the addition of the three genomics companies, 190 entities are now listed. Goods affected include everything from cotton and canned tomatoes to electronics.

title: Bank of Canada raises key interest rate, says another hike possible
full_text:
By Promit Mukherjee and David Ljunggren
OTTAWA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The Bank of Canada on Wednesday hiked its key policy rate for the first time in more than three years and said further increases might be needed to prevent soaring energy costs from fueling broader inflation.
The bank lifted the rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%, as widely expected, and also ramped up its inflation forecast for 2027 to 3.1% from the 2.0% it had predicted in July. Growth this year is set to be 1.0%, higher than the 0.7% seen in July.
"With the outlook for inflation substantially higher and the economy showing resilience, an increase in the policy rate is needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalized inflation," Governor Tiff Macklem said in opening remarks to reporters.
"There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, we will proceed carefully."
The rate increase would likely push up bank lending rates and mortgage costs and could slow economic growth. But Macklem said he was trying to ensure costs stay contained.
"Higher interest rates aren’t going to immediately feel like they are helping," Macklem said.
"What is the best thing we can do for Canadian households and Canadian businesses... is that we can get inflation down," he said.
The annual inflation rate hit 3.2% in September, above the bank’s 1%-3% target range, almost solely led by higher energy and energy-related costs of transportation.
Macklem said inflation was expected to end the year at 3.5% and stay around 3% for most of next year before returning close to the 2% target by the middle of 2028.
The rate hike was the first since July 2023.
Despite the increase, the rate is still below the mid-point of the neutral rate, a monetary policy level which is neither considered restrictive or accommodative. The BoC considers the mid-point at 2.75%.
Macklem, during his press conference, said that while the policy rate was still slightly accommodative he will not prejudge where he would want the rate to be in coming months.
"There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but we are very mindful that there is a lot of uncertainty and against that background there is no predetermined path," he said.
Money markets are pricing in another 25 basis point rate cut in January and see the benchmark rate going up to 3.25% by December next year.
"We don’t expect that core measures of inflation will accelerate as much as the Bank fears, particularly if global energy prices ease a little, and as a result we don’t think that the policy rate will need to move above 2.75%," said Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Capital Markets.
Past experience and the BoC’s surveys suggest that cost pass-through will increase over the next year, increasing overall inflation, Macklem said.
Economists who opposed a hike said core inflation, which strips out the cost of volatile items, is still hovering around 2%. They also say a rate hike could impede modest economic recovery, given US trade tensions and a weak job market.
Macklem said new US tariffs would slow the economy in the fourth quarter, but expressed confidence that growth should pick up again in 2027 as consumer spending continues, exports pick up and business investment strengthens.
After a robust annualized growth of 3.3% in the second quarter, the economy is likely to slow to 2% in the third quarter and further down to 0.8% in Q4, the BoC’s new monetary policy report projected.
The report, however, upgraded its GDP forecast for next year and year after to 2% from 1.8% for both 2027 and 2028 as predicted in July.
The Canadian dollar firmed slightly and was trading at C$1.4050 to the US dollar, or 71.17 US cents.
The BoC’s next rate decision is on December 9.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at the post-decision press conference said that conditions on the employment side of the central bank’s dual mandate were "quite positive" and that the Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) discussion focused mainly on the inflation side. Warsh added that the Fed had also seen some tightening of financial conditions and more discerning market participants since the FOMC’s September meeting.
The FOMC maintained the federal funds rate at 3.75%-4.00% in a 10-2 vote, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack preferring a quarter-point hike instead. The FOMC had raised the key policy rate by 25 basis points at its last meeting in September, marking the first instance of monetary policy tightening since July 2023.
"Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little," the FOMC said in a statement.
"Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability," the statement added.
The Fed held rates steady despite hotter-than-expected inflation readings recently. The headline U.S. consumer price index (CPI) climbed 3.7% Y/Y in September, while the core CPI - which strips out food and energy - gained 2.6% Y/Y. Both figures accelerated from August’s readings of 3.4% and 2.4%, respectively, and were well above the Fed’s long-term target of 2%.
The FOMC prefers to track the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index as its gauge of inflation. The latest PCE reading for August showed a rise of 3.4% Y/Y, while core PCE ticked up 3%.
Warsh at the press conference once again declined against providing forward guidance, a trait that he has become famous for. The Fed chair also noted that there was crucial economic data scheduled in the days ahead, and that the information received "over the coming period will help us determine where policy will be."
Watchers of monetary policy will indeed receive Q3 U.S. gross domestic product data and the September reading on the PCE as soon as Thursday.
"The period right in front of us is information rich," Warsh said, adding that "in this coming period, we’re going to be able to figure out what’s the appropriate protocol…to deliver price stability. I’m encouraged by the progress we’ve made in a short period of time."
The Middle East conflict continues to be a volatile supply shock, boosting global energy prices. A jump in the index for gasoline prices contributed to over half of the monthly rise in U.S. headline CPI in September.
Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury yields have soared to multi-decade highs since the Fed’s last meeting in September, driving up borrowing costs and effectively doing the same job as a rate hike would have.
"The Federal Reserve kept rates unchanged Wednesday as it would prefer to assess more incoming economic data and avoid making policy changes so close to the midterm elections. While bond yields have cooled off, they surged in the weeks following the Fed’s September rate hike, suggesting that the markets have done plenty of tightening for the Fed already," Rick Gardner, chief investment officer at RGA Investments, said.
"The Federal Reserve knows that the tools in its toolbox can’t control energy prices, which are such a big driver of inflation, so it would rather hike rates carefully and slowly, instead of embarking on a swift hiking cycle," he added.
Watchers of monetary policy expect the Fed to restart hiking in December. The minutes of the Fed’s September meeting had shown that most policymakers saw another rate increase by the end of this year.
Warsh also announced a change in the FOMC’s meeting schedule for 2027 and 2028. While the committee will continue to hold eight meetings, one of those meetings next year will focus on monetary policy strategy instead of delivering a decision on the federal funds rate. That will expand to two meetings in 2028.
The Fed chair also touched upon the U.S. midterm elections. When asked if the polls were a factor in Wednesday’s rate decision, Warsh said "politics played no role" in the move.

title: Cerebras Systems drops 4% following Culper Research short report

Investing.com -- Shares of Cerebras Systems (NYSE: CBRS) slid 4% on Wednesday after Culper Research disclosed a short position, publishing a critical report that questions the durability and underlying technology of the AI chipmaker’s flagship wafer-scale engines.
At the core of Culper’s thesis is the allegation that Cerebras’s massive chips have a functional lifespan of just 1.5 to 2.5 years in the field, a limitation the firm argues fundamentally undermines the company’s business model.
The report specifically challenges claims made by Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman regarding the invention of a novel connector material to solve thermal expansion issues. According to Culper, Cerebras actually relies on PariPoser—a material developed in the 1980s and sold by Paricon Technologies. The short seller claims Paricon confirmed that PariPoser is utilized in Cerebras’s delivered products, contradicting the narrative of a proprietary in-house breakthrough.
Furthermore, Culper alleges that Cerebras purposefully programs its wafers to run continuous "dummy operations" to prevent them from ever cooling down. The report points to a June 2026 Café Compute event in Berlin, where a Cerebras solutions architect reportedly admitted that these dummy operations are necessary to keep the hardware functional, as allowing the chips to cool could cause them to break.
Supporting this claim, Culper stated that a decompilation of Cerebras’s client-side software uncovered a field labeled "dummy tokens," which the firm noted is distinct from standard padding tokens and absent in comparable software from competitors like Nvidia, Google, and Intel.
Culper argues this workaround trades one engineering hurdle for another, causing wafers that are never allowed to cool to degrade rapidly in the field. Cerebras has historically touted its wafer-scale integration as the ultimate solution to a 75-year-old industry challenge of building, powering, and cooling a processor the size of an entire silicon wafer.
Cerebras Systems has not yet issued a public response to the allegations.

title: Nvidia faces DOJ antitrust scrutiny over $12.9B Hugging Face deal, Reuters says

Investing.com -- The U.S. Department of Justice is probing NVIDIA Corporation's (NASDAQ:NVDA) planned $12.93 billion acquisition of open-source artificial intelligence hub Hugging Face, folding questions about the transaction into a broader, multi-year antitrust investigation into the chipmaker's business practices, Reuters reported. Shares of Nvidia slipped 1.7% in Wednesday trading following the news, as market participants weighed the regulatory headwinds facing the world's premier computing firm.
Antitrust enforcers have zeroed in on whether absorbing Hugging Face would allow Nvidia to seize control of a crucial distribution channel for AI models and software, according to two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia, which anticipates closing the transaction in the first half of 2027, has maintained that the platform will preserve open support across a full spectrum of rival processors, cloud architectures, and software ecosystems.
Beyond the pending Hugging Face buyout, federal investigators are scrutinizing Nvidia’s sales tactics, strategic investments, and historical acquisitions to evaluate whether the company has exerted undue commercial pressure on customers. Regulatory questions have targeted Nvidia’s prior purchases of workload-orchestration developer Run:ai and supercomputing software firm SchedMD, alongside a 2025 licensing and talent arrangement with chip startup Groq.
Of particular interest to officials is whether Nvidia leveraged its dominant graphics processing units to compel buyers into taking adjacent products, exploring allegations that preferential chip allocations were tied to purchases of its networking equipment and Groq processors. Such practices would signal an effort to fortify a walled ecosystem at a time when rivals such as Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, and Alphabet are expanding their custom silicon initiatives.
The sweeping conduct inquiry originated under the Biden administration and has extended into the Trump presidency, reflecting a staff-led regulatory review that has spanned multiple political cycles. Although President Donald Trump has praised Nvidia's leadership and awarded Chief Executive Jensen Huang the National Medal of Science, there is no indication the White House has intervened, and inquiries do not inevitably lead to formal legal enforcement.
A Justice Department spokesperson declined to address specific matters before the agency, emphasizing that leadership prioritizes domestic superintelligence capabilities while noting that conduct investigations are distinct from routine merger reviews. For investors, the intensifying scrutiny underscores a critical friction point for Nvidia, testing its ability to deploy massive cash reserves toward vertical integration without triggering heightened regulatory resistance.

title: Is Zuckerberg pulling the rug out from under Anthropic?
full_text:
Investing.com -- Meta Platforms is making an extraordinarily expensive push into artificial intelligence, and the timing could hardly be more challenging for Anthropic.
Just as the Claude developer prepares for what it hopes could be the largest initial public offering ever, Mark Zuckerberg’s company is raising as much as $97.5 billion to accelerate its own AI ambitions.
The collision comes at a particularly sensitive moment: Anthropic’s newly released IPO prospectus reveals explosive revenue growth and improving profitability, but also enormous future spending commitments that make continued access to capital essential.
Meanwhile, Meta’s newest AI models are beginning to rival Claude on important performance benchmarks, often at significantly lower prices.
The central question for potential IPO investors is no longer who has the smartest and fastest-growing AI, but whether Anthropic can build a sustainable technological and economic lead against a rival with vastly greater financial resources, an established global distribution network and a willingness to spend and price dump aggressively.
Anthropic’s extraordinary growth comes with an extraordinary price tag
Anthropic’s financial disclosures offer one of the clearest pictures yet of the economics behind the AI boom: according to its IPO prospectus, the company generated $16.29 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026, compared with just $1.16 billion a year earlier.
More importantly, its operating loss narrowed to $693 million, while adjusted operating income turned positive at $1.62 billion. That is meaningful progress for a company spending billions to develop frontier AI models.
The headline net loss of $80.7 billion looks considerably worse, although roughly $72.4 billion reflects a noncash accounting charge related to the rising value of convertible financing instruments rather than money lost through everyday operations.
Still, the real challenge lies ahead.
Anthropic has entered over $600 billion in compute and infrastructure agreements stretching over the coming years. Those are not all immediately payable, and some are contingent on capacity delivery, but they illustrate the extraordinary scale of future investment.
Amazon and Alphabet are central to that strategy, providing both capital and access to computing infrastructure - and while the backing gives Anthropic substantial resources, it also leaves the company dependent on continued growth, infrastructure availability and the willingness of investors and partners to keep the capital flowing.
Zuckerberg’s $97.5 billion challenge
Meta on October 27 expanded its massive equity financing initiative to $97.5 billion, including $25 billion in common stock priced at $625 per share and $12.5 billion in preferred securities.
A further at-the-market offering of up to $60 billion is planned following the expected launch of Meta’s nonvoting Class C shares in early 2027.
Chipmakers Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have also expressed interest in participating in the financing, underscoring how closely interconnected the industry’s capital and infrastructure investments have become.
The result is an unusually direct competition for investor capital.
Anthropic is preparing to ask institutional investors to assign an enormous valuation to a rapidly growing but still capital-intensive AI developer. At virtually the same time, Meta is offering investors exposure to an established technology giant pouring billions into its own AI expansion.
Meta’s spending is not without consequences: the company reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion in the third quarter, compared with positive cash flow of $10.63 billion a year earlier, while raising its full-year capital expenditure forecast to between $135 billion and $145 billion.
But Zuckerberg has one advantage Anthropic cannot easily replicate: Meta’s established advertising business generates substantial revenue and cash flow that can help fund continued AI development.
For Anthropic, raising capital remains central to building its business. For Meta, AI investment can also be supported by an enormous business that already exists.
Meta’s most dangerous weapon may be its pricing
Money alone does not guarantee technological superiority, but Meta is increasingly demonstrating that it may not need the best AI to become a formidable competitor.
Anthropic’s Claude models remain among the industry’s leaders in advanced reasoning, coding and enterprise applications. Yet independent benchmarks published in October show Meta’s Muse models closing the gap across several important categories.
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Muse Wonder Full scored 56, matching Claude Sonnet 5.5 and trailing Claude Opus 5.5’s score of 58.
Claude retained a meaningful advantage on the ProgramBench coding evaluation, while Meta’s model outperformed it on the longer-duration SWE-Marathon test.
The results are mixed, but the broader implication is difficult to ignore: Meta is already delivering competitive AI capabilities without consistently matching Anthropic’s most advanced models.
And it is doing so at substantially lower published prices.
Meta’s Muse Spark 1.3 costs $1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 per million output tokens, compared with $4 and $20, respectively, for Claude Opus 5.5.
The models are not directly equivalent in capability, and the total cost of completing a task can differ from their per-token pricing. Nonetheless, Meta is establishing itself as an aggressive lower-cost alternative.
For enterprise customers, this could become increasingly difficult to ignore.
A business using AI to process hunderds of thousands of customer inquiries, analyze documents or perform routine coding tasks may find that a slightly less capable model is more than sufficient, particularly when the cost difference becomes substantial at scale.
The threat to Anthropic is therefore not theoretical: as competing models become capable enough to handle more commercial workloads, the number of applications in which Claude can command a meaningful premium could begin to shrink.
And for a company seeking a valuation of $1.5 trillion or more, simply hoping to remain a little better than everyone else is a questionable long-term strategy.
Is Meta actually cheaper, or just willing to lose money?
There is, however, an important distinction between offering AI at a lower price and actually producing it more efficiently.
Meta has not publicly disclosed sufficiently detailed unit economics for its Muse models to establish whether its aggressive pricing reflects a durable cost advantage or just its willingness to sacrifice profitability to gain market share.
There are reasons to believe its technology is becoming more efficient. Meta has emphasized improvements in model architecture, inference optimization and utilization of computing infrastructure.
Zuckerberg also said during Meta’s latest earnings call that the company expects to improve Muse’s compute cost efficiency by more than tenfold over the next year.
But those are projections, not proof that Muse is already cheaper to operate than Claude - Zuckerberg openly has acknowledged that Muse remains unprofitable and requires enormous resources to operate and improve.
Independent benchmarks also suggest the pricing comparison is more complicated than it first appears: although Muse Spark’s per-token prices are considerably lower, some evaluations show that it consumes significantly more tokens to complete comparable tasks. That can narrow or even eliminate the cost advantage on an individual assignment.
In other words, Meta may be selling AI more cheaply without necessarily producing each successful result more cheaply.
Yet that distinction offers Anthropic only limited comfort.
Even if Meta is effectively subsidizing AI usage, it has the financial resources to sustain aggressive pricing for a considerable period - in the third quarter alone, Meta generated $32.79 billion in operating cash flow, supported overwhelmingly by its established advertising operations.
That cash flow is under pressure from enormous infrastructure spending, and Meta is itself turning to equity markets for additional capital, but, unlike Anthropic, it does not need its AI products to generate sufficient revenue to support the entire business.
Zuckerberg can also justify AI investment through benefits that do not appear directly in Muse’s revenue, including improved advertising performance, user engagement and commerce.
For Anthropic, the economics are considerably less forgiving. Selling access to AI is its central business, and continued investment in increasingly expensive infrastructure depends on making that business financially sustainable.
Even if Meta’s pricing strategy proves unprofitable in the near term, Anthropic still faces the challenge of competing against a company that can potentially absorb those losses for longer.
The bull case: Anthropic can fight back, but not on technology alone
None of this means Anthropic is destined to lose.
In fact, its IPO disclosures provide considerable evidence that it has already built a viable commercial foundation: revenue is seeing extraordinary growth, operating losses have narrowed substantially, and adjusted operating income has turned positive.
Those improvements suggest Anthropic is learning to convert technical capabilities into a more efficient business, rather than simply spending ever larger amounts to produce better models.
Sustaining that progress, however, will require more than defending Claude’s position at the top of AI leaderboards.
One potential response is to compete on efficiency itself.
Anthropic can reduce inference costs through improved model architectures, more efficient use of computing capacity and increasingly capable smaller models. It can also lower prices where necessary while reserving premium pricing for workloads that genuinely require its most advanced technology.
This is particularly important because a technological lead is not automatically an economic moat. If achieving slightly better benchmark results requires substantially more spending, that lead may eventually become too expensive to maintain.
Another opportunity lies in moving beyond selling access to models.
Anthropic’s growing enterprise relationships, development tools and integration into corporate workflows offer potential ways to make Claude more valuable than the underlying technology alone.
A business that has embedded Claude into its software development processes, internal systems and employee workflows may be less inclined to switch providers simply because another model is cheaper.
That would allow Anthropic to compete increasingly on the value of its broader ecosystem rather than the price of individual tokens.
Its partnerships with Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud also provide access to enterprise distribution channels and substantial infrastructure resources.
And while these arrangements create dependencies, they give Anthropic a path to scale without building every part of its commercial ecosystem independently.
The strongest bullish scenario is therefore not one in which Claude remains the world’s most capable model indefinitely, but one in which Anthropic uses its technological position and early commercial success to build a business that customers find difficult to replace, while steadily bringing down the cost of delivering its technology.
The bear case: Meta can afford a longer price war
The more troubling scenario is one in which Meta continues narrowing the performance gap while maintaining its substantially lower prices.
At that point, Anthropic may face an increasingly uncomfortable choice: protect margins and risk losing customers, or match competitors’ prices and sacrifice profitability.
Neither option is particularly attractive for a company with hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure agreements and substantial future financing requirements.
There is also a potentially damaging feedback loop: if Anthropic lowers prices to remain competitive, it may need to sell significantly more AI usage to generate the same revenue. That additional demand could require greater computing capacity, particularly if efficiency improvements fail to keep pace with price reductions, resulting in a business growing rapidly in usage but struggling to translate that growth into sustainable profits.
Meta, meanwhile, could continue using its advertising cash flow to support AI investment, even if its models take longer to become profitable.
That does not make the company immune to financial pressure: its own CapEx have grown enormously, free cash flow has turned negative, and shareholders are already questioning the scale of Zuckerberg’s spending.
But Meta has considerably more flexibility in how it monetizes AI and how long it can tolerate weak direct returns.
Its distribution network compounds that advantage. Zuckerberg said during the company’s latest earnings call that Meta serves approximately 500 million businesses across its platforms, providing a potentially enormous cross- and upselling opportunity.
For Anthropic, the risk is that AI capabilities become increasingly interchangeable before it has established enough customer loyalty, proprietary workflows and cost advantages to defend its business.
And if Meta can produce comparable models at genuinely lower costs, rather than merely subsidizing prices, the challenge becomes more serious still.
The IPO adds another layer of pressure
Anthropic’s planned Nasdaq debut, expected before Thanksgiving under the ticker ANT, could raise as much as $100 billion and value the business between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.
But valuation expectations have already become less certain as investors reassess the industry’s spending requirements and competitive outlook, making Meta’s financing particularly significant.
The companies are not necessarily seeking capital from identical investors, and Meta’s proposed $60 billion at-the-market program would be spread over time rather than raised in a single offering.
Nevertheless, both are asking financial markets to fund enormous AI ambitions at a time when investors are becoming increasingly selective.
For Anthropic, the stakes extend far beyond the success of a single listing: the company’s long-term ability to compete will depend not just on generating revenue, but on raising enough capital at attractive terms to fund infrastructure, development and expansion.
A successful IPO would strengthen its balance sheet and provide additional financial flexibility.
But even a strong debut would not resolve the fundamental challenge of competing against a rival that can fund AI investment through a much larger, established business.
A disappointing valuation, meanwhile, could make future financing significantly more expensive, particularly if investors begin questioning whether Anthropic can defend its tech lead and pricing power.
That makes the IPO an unusually important test of whether financial markets believe an independent AI developer can sustain its position against the world’s largest technology companies.
Bottom line: Anthropic needs more than the best AI
Anthropic has already demonstrated that it can build world-class AI technology and turn it into a rapidly growing commercial business. Its improving operating results suggest the company is much more than an expensive research experiment.
But Meta is challenging the assumption that superior AI technology necessarily translates into durable pricing power, and Zuckerberg is ready to deploy his empire’s full financial resources to narrow the gap.
Whether Muse’s low prices reflect genuine efficiency gains or deliberate margin sacrifices remains unclear, but one thing is certain: Meta has the resources, distribution and existing cash-generating businesses to sustain aggressive competition.
Anthropic can counter that challenge through better economics, stronger enterprise relationships and products that customers value beyond their underlying models, but it cannot just rely on remaining slightly ahead on benchmarks and charging substantially more.
For a company seeking a valuation of as high as $2 trillion and facing extraordinary future infrastructure commitments, technological superiority alone is unlikely to be enough.
The IPO will provide an early verdict.

title: Oracle eases AI spending worries with plan to turn cash flow positive
full_text:
Oct 28 (Reuters) - Oracle said on Wednesday it expects capital spending to peak this fiscal year and next as it builds more cloud-computing capacity, but pledged to raise no more than $20 billion in additional financing through fiscal 2030.
The pledge is meant to reassure investors worried that Larry Ellison’s company will need ever-larger sums of outside money to fund its aggressive AI buildout. Oracle shares jumped over 12% on the forecasts, while other cloud stocks also rose.
Speaking at Oracle’s investor day in Las Vegas, CFO Hilary Maxson said Oracle also expects free cash flow to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and top $30 billion in fiscal 2029, when capital spending is set to decline.
Oracle has become a focal point of worries about the soaring cost of AI infrastructure because it lacks the deep revenue base of cloud giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and relies heavily on a single customer, loss-making ChatGPT creator OpenAI.
The partnership with OpenAI has added hundreds of billions of dollars to Oracle’s cloud backlog, but building the data centers and other AI infrastructure needed to fulfill those contracts has forced it to lean heavily on debt and stock sales.
PLANS TO CUT BACK ON OUTSIDE FINANCING
Oracle said on Wednesday it expects vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer pre-payments to reduce its upfront cash needs until free cash flow turns positive.
It expects to stop relying on outside funding for growth from fiscal 2029, with net debt forecast to fall below 3.5 times its annual core earnings that year.
The company said earlier this year it would raise $40 billion through debt and equity financing in its current fiscal year, including the $20 billion stock sale it completed in the first quarter.
It had $125.34 billion in notes payable and other borrowings as of August 31, while cash and cash equivalents totaled around $36.37 billion.
"I’ve told you we need an additional up to $20 billion in funding for the remainder of our fiscal 2027," CFO Maxson said on Wednesday.
"We’re announcing that this $20 billion, split evenly between debt and equity, is the final amount needed to fund the remainder of this cycle."
Oracle’s five-year credit default swaps, which measure the cost of insuring against a default on its debt, were down marginally at 287.2 basis points on Wednesday.
Maxson’s remarks lifted shares of AI cloud and infrastructure companies after weeks of selling pressure over worries that the AI boom is becoming too dependent on debt.
CoreWeave, Nebius, Applied Digital and Iren gained between 2.1% and 5%.
For fiscal 2030, Oracle forecast revenue of more than $225 billion, an adjusted operating margin above 40% and adjusted earnings of more than $21 per share. It reaffirmed its fiscal 2027 forecast of more than $90 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings of $8.10 per share.
